live.name: NICKEL FOXCROFT
live.headline: NICKEL FOXCROFT: a threat actor known by many names
live.in_short: The catalogue lists NICKEL FOXCROFT under many aliases, including APT37 and ScarCruft, and names eight tools tied to it. No public report in this library describes its operations.

sentences.t: NICKEL FOXCROFT is the Secureworks name for a threat actor tracked under many other names.
Its aliases include APT37, ATK4, Group 123, InkySquid, Moldy Pisces, Operation Daybreak, Operaton Erebus, RICOCHET CHOLLIMA, Reaper, ScarCruft, TA-RedAnt and Venus 121.
The catalogue links eight tools to the actor: Bluelight, Chinotto, GOLDBACKDOOR, KevDroid, KoSpy, PoorWeb, ROKRAT and final1stpy.
No public report in this library describes its operations.

next.name: NICKEL FOXCROFT
next.headline: NICKEL FOXCROFT (APT37, ScarCruft): a long-running espionage group focused on Korea
next.in_short: NICKEL FOXCROFT, also tracked as APT37 and ScarCruft, is described by vendors as a North Korea-linked espionage group. Its reported tools reach air-gapped networks, game platforms and Android phones.

sentences.t: Secureworks tracks this actor as NICKEL FOXCROFT. Other names for it include APT37, ScarCruft, Reaper, Group 123, InkySquid, Moldy Pisces, Venus 121 and TA-RedAnt.
ESET says ScarCruft, also known as APT37 or Reaper, has operated since at least 2012. ESET suspects it is a North Korean espionage group.
CrowdStrike calls its version of the actor RICOCHET CHOLLIMA and describes it as a DPRK-nexus targeted intrusion adversary. It dates the espionage to at least 2016.

Lookout describes ScarCruft as a North Korean state-sponsored cyber espionage group active since 2012. It also notes that North Korean groups share infrastructure, targeting and techniques, which makes attribution harder.
CrowdStrike says the actor's observed operations have almost exclusively targeted the Republic of Korea. It assesses the focus to be government officials, NGOs, academics and journalists.

ESET says the group primarily focuses on South Korea, though other Asian countries have also been targeted. It says the group seems mainly interested in government and military organisations, and in companies in various sectors.
In a recent case ESET infers the main targets were ethnic Koreans in Yanbian, China, most likely refugees or defectors.
Kudelski Security and Sekoia say a related cluster, Reaper, focuses on DPRK defectors and South Korean activists and NGOs.
Zscaler ThreatLabz says APT37 has abused shortcut (LNK) files as an initial way in for years.
Reported tools include ROKRAT, Bluelight, KoSpy and others.

S2W described a 2020 watering-hole attack that ended in a ROKRAT variant. The malware used legitimate cloud services such as pCloud, Yandex, Box, Dropbox and Backblaze B2 for command and control. S2W judges the activity to relate to ScarCruft.
Zscaler's report says that, to its knowledge, this was the first time APT37 abused Zoho WorkDrive for command and control.

In the Ruby Jumper campaign, Zscaler describes malware that spreads over removable media to reach air-gapped networks. A malicious shortcut file starts the chain, and a tool called THUMBSBD carries commands and stolen data over USB media.

ESET reports that ScarCruft trojanized Windows and Android parts of a video game platform aimed at Yanbian, China. The goal was to deliver its BirdCall backdoor, which can collect files, contacts, SMS and voice recordings. ESET says the attack was probably under way since late 2024.

Lookout attributes the KoSpy Android spyware to ScarCruft (APT37) with medium confidence. The apps posed as utilities and were distributed through Google Play. Lookout says the samples date from March 2022 to March 2024.

Researcher Doron Karmi described 2019 campaigns using the Konni remote administration tool, which Karmi says is potentially linked to APT37. Karmi could not confirm every overlap with related tooling.
Organisations in the sectors named above should treat unexpected shortcut files and unfamiliar removable media with caution.
Apps should come only from trusted sources, and software updates should be checked before they are installed.
